articles.title: Victims of Sexual Abuse
articles.author: Sejal Desai
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. Yes, children can become victims of sexual abuse through online gaming platforms. Offenders use in-game chat, voice features, and private messages to build trust with children and then push them toward sexual contact or explicit images. California is the most populous state in the country and one of the world’s largest economies. It is home to Silicon Valley and many of the world’s best-known technology and video game companies. Major game studios operate in both the San Francisco Bay Area and Southern California. With so many popular games built there, online safety is a growing concern for families across the state. When a child is harmed, some parents speak with a child sex abuse lawyer in California to learn how offenders and others can be held accountable. How Gaming Platforms Create Risk Many games let children talk with strangers in real time, which gives offenders direct access to young users. Common risk points include: Open text and voice chat with unknown players Private messaging and friend requests In-game gifts, currency, or rare items Offenders often move the child from the game to a less monitored messaging or video app, where contact is harder to spot. What Grooming Often Looks Like Grooming is gradual. An offender builds a close bond so the child feels special or indebted. Warning Signs in the Online Relationship Parents may notice patterns such as: An older “friend” who gives frequent gifts or game currency Requests to keep the friendship secret Requests for photos or video calls Changes in the Child’s Behavior A groomed child may become secretive about devices or upset when gaming is limited. Some show sudden mood changes, withdraw from family, or have new items they cannot explain. In some cases, offenders demand more images by threatening to share photos the child already sent. This crime is often called sextortion. What Federal Law Says Online child exploitation is a federal crime. Under 18 U.S.C. § 2422(b), it is illegal to use the internet to persuade or entice a minor into sexual activity, and the offense carries a mandatory minimum of 10 years in prison. Victims also have civil options. Under 18 U.S.C. § 2255, a person exploited as a minor can sue the offender for damages of at least $150,000 plus attorney’s fees. Can Gaming Companies Be Held Responsible? Platform liability is more complex. A federal law known as Section 230, found at 47 U.S.C. § 230, often protects online platforms from liability for content posted by users. Recent lawsuits against gaming and chat companies argue that unsafe product design, weak age checks, and poor safety tools contributed to harm. Courts are still deciding these claims . Steps to Take If You Suspect Abuse Acting quickly can stop the contact and protect evidence. These steps can help: Block the offender, but do not delete the account or messages. Record usernames, dates, and screenshots of chats that do not contain explicit images. Report the activity to NCMEC’s CyberTipline and local law enforcement. Report the user to the gaming platform. Connect your child with a counselor who works with abuse survivors. Never copy, save, or forward explicit images of a child, even as evidence. Police can collect them directly. Key Takeaways Children can be sexually abused through contact that begins on gaming platforms. Offenders often use chat, gifts, secrecy, and threats to exploit young players. 18 U.S.C. § 2422(b) makes online enticement of a minor a federal crime. Victims may seek civil damages under 18 U.S.C. § 2255. Section 230 can limit platform liability, but courts are testing design-based claims. Preserving evidence and reporting quickly help protect the child and the case.

articles.title: Fantasy Sports Can Teach
articles.author: Tiqua Jackson
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. The Draft Is Only the Beginning Every fall, fantasy managers spend weeks preparing for a single evening. They study rankings, run mock drafts, and argue over the first pick. Then the season starts, and most of them learn that draft night settles very little. Injuries pile up, bye weeks arrive, and the waiver wire fills with players nobody saw coming. Matthew Bissell, a lifelong football, baseball, and basketball fan who plays in fantasy leagues, recognizes that cycle. As a financial consultant with The Broker Group, he watches families treat a financial plan the way many managers treat the draft: something to finish once and set aside. A plan built at one point in life reflects the information available at that moment. Jobs change, children grow, and priorities shift. For an Oakland financial consultant who works with clients on life insurance and retirement questions, the comparison helps because so many people already get it. A fantasy team needs attention all season. So does a household budget, a retirement account, or a life insurance policy. Building a Roster That Can Absorb an Injury Experienced fantasy players learn to draft depth. A roster built entirely around one star can collapse the week that player goes down, while a roster with dependable backups keeps competing. Families face a similar question with far higher stakes. If a household depends on one or two incomes, the plan has to account for what happens if one of those incomes stops. Life insurance is one tool people use to address that risk, and it works best when it fits the family it protects: the number of dependents, the size of the mortgage or rent, and the years until the children are on their own. The roster comparison also helps people see protection as part of the plan from the start. Fantasy managers don't wait until their starting running back is hurt to look for a replacement. By then, the best options are usually gone. Depth has to be revisited, too. A roster that made sense in September can look thin by November, and coverage chosen before a new baby, a new home, or a career change may no longer fit. A quick review after each major life event keeps the plan matched to the family as it is today. Matthew Bissell on Patience Over Weekly Swings Anyone who has managed a fantasy team knows the temptation to overreact. A player has one bad game and gets dropped, then scores big the following week for someone else. Managers who trade away proven players after a slow start often regret it by midseason. Retirement savings test the same instinct. Market headlines can make a single rough month feel like a crisis, and the urge to pull money out or change course entirely is strong. Steady, long-term retirement planning guidance looks at the full season instead of one bad week: set goals that match a person's age and timeline, contribute consistently, and review the plan on a schedule instead of in moments of worry. Patience comes easier when the plan is clear. A manager who knows why each player is on the roster is less likely to panic. A saver who understands why money sits in a particular account is more likely to leave it there and let time do its work. Read the League Rules Before the Season Starts Every fantasy league has its own scoring system, roster limits, and trade deadlines. Players who skip the rules find out the hard way that their league rewards different things than the rankings they studied. Financial products come with rules too. Life insurance policies have terms, coverage periods, and conditions. Retirement accounts have contribution limits, withdrawal rules, and timelines. Clients don't need to become experts, but they should understand what they own and how it works. A good consultant spends much of the conversation explaining those details in plain language, answering questions, and making sure nothing in the paperwork comes as a surprise later. Matthew Bissell draws here on a career spent in service roles. Before moving into financial consulting in 2025, he worked in community support positions in San Francisco and Oakland, helping people work through practical needs one step at a time. That background shapes how he runs a client meeting: listen first, explain clearly, and give people enough information to make their own decisions. Bringing the Whole Family Into the Conversation Some of the best fantasy leagues are the ones played with family and friends. The trash talk is half the fun, and the season gives people a reason to stay in touch every week. Financial planning can benefit from the same openness. Many households leave money decisions to one person, so a spouse or adult child ends up unsure where things stand if something changes. Talking through the plan together, even briefly, means everyone knows what coverage exists, where retirement savings are held, and what the family is working toward. As a father of two, Bissell knows these conversations come down to one question: whether the people who matter most will be cared for, whatever the season brings. A Plan That Lasts the Whole Season Fantasy football ends in December. A family's financial life has no off-season. The habits that help fantasy managers compete through the playoffs, such as building depth, staying patient, learning the rules, and keeping everyone involved, are the same habits that help families stay prepared over decades. For Matthew Bissell, both teach the same lesson. Preparation matters, but steady attention after the draft is what carries a team, or a household, through the end of the year and well beyond.

articles.title: Split King Adjustable Bed
articles.author: Britta Hedlund
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. When two people share a bed but follow different bedtime routines, comfort can become a matter of timing as much as mattress choice. One person may settle down early, while the other stays up reading, watching television, or finishing work. Later, the second person may climb into bed and change positions several times before falling asleep. These ordinary differences can affect how each person experiences movement, pressure, and support throughout the night. A split king setup offers a practical way to manage different resting preferences, particularly when one sleeper likes an elevated upper body while the other prefers a flatter position. However, separate adjustment does not eliminate every shared-bed concern. The mattress still needs to respond to body weight, movement, and changes in pressure, while the bedding must accommodate the way each person rests. Understanding what happens to memory foam between positions can help couples make better decisions about their sleeping arrangements without assuming that a different bed angle will automatically solve every comfort issue. When Two Bedtime Routines Meet in One Bedroom Different sleep schedules can create small challenges that become more noticeable over time. The earlier sleeper may already be comfortable and close to falling asleep when the other person enters the room, turns on a reading light, or adjusts the bedding. Even if both people are careful, getting into bed can transfer movement through the mattress and interrupt the first sleeper's rest. The effect depends on the mattress construction, the amount of movement, and how sensitive each person is to disturbance. The challenge is not limited to movement. One person might prefer to sleep with the upper body raised, while the other finds a flat position more comfortable. One may use a thick blanket, while the other prefers a light cover. A split king adjustable bed can help accommodate these differences by allowing each side to be positioned independently. Before choosing such a setup, however, couples should consider how the mattress responds to pressure and movement, how much separation exists between the two sides, and whether the arrangement suits their usual sleeping habits. How a Split King Adjustable Bed Handles Different Positions A split king adjustable bed generally uses two separate sleeping surfaces or independently adjustable sides arranged to form a king-size sleeping area. This arrangement allows one person to raise the head or legs without requiring the other person to adopt the same position. For couples with different routines, that flexibility can be useful when one person reads in bed, rests with elevated legs, or prefers a different angle while settling down. The important distinction is that independent movement does not mean every part of the sleep experience becomes independent. The two sleepers may still share a room, blankets, or other bedding, and movement can sometimes be felt across the sleeping surface depending on the mattress and frame design. The center area between the two sides may also feel different from the outer edges. Understanding these details helps set realistic expectations: separate adjustment can make individual positioning easier, but the quality of the mattress and the fit of the bedding still matter. What Memory Foam Does When One Person Moves Memory foam responds gradually when pressure is applied. As someone lies down, the foam compresses beneath heavier contact points and conforms to the body's shape. When that person changes position, the material begins to recover, although the speed and degree of recovery depend on the foam's formulation, temperature, and construction. This response is one reason memory foam can feel different when someone first lies down compared with after remaining in the same position for several minutes. In a shared bed, the experience also depends on how much movement reaches the other sleeper. Some mattress designs absorb movement more effectively than others, but performance varies according to construction and the force of the movement. When one person enters bed late, the initial compression and repositioning may be more noticeable than small movements made after both people are settled. A mattress that limits motion transfer can help reduce disturbance, although it cannot guarantee that a sensitive sleeper will never notice another person's movements. Why Pressure Can Change Between Evening and Morning The body does not maintain exactly the same position throughout the night. Sleepers turn onto their sides, move onto their backs, bend their knees, or adjust their shoulders to find a more comfortable position. Each movement changes the areas pressing against the mattress. Memory foam responds to those changes, gradually compressing in new places and recovering where pressure has been removed. As a result, a mattress can feel supportive in one position but less comfortable in another. For example, a side sleeper may feel more pressure around the shoulder and hip, while a back sleeper may notice support differently around the pelvis and lower back. Raising the upper body changes the angle of the torso and can alter how the shoulders meet the mattress. Elevating the legs can also change the position of the knees and hips. Rather than judging a mattress from one brief position, it is more useful to consider how it feels across the positions a person actually uses, including the transition between them. The Mattress Construction Behind Everyday Comfort Foam density, comfort-layer thickness, firmness, and surface materials all contribute to how a mattress responds when someone settles into bed. Softer comfort layers may allow more sinking around the shoulders and hips, while firmer constructions can provide a different balance of contouring and resistance. Neither approach is ideal for every sleeper. Body weight, sleeping position, personal preference, and the support provided by the underlying foundation all influence the final experience. The SweetNight CoolNest Mattress is one option to examine when comparing mattress construction and everyday sleeping comfort. Reviewing its product details can help readers understand its design and assess whether it aligns with their preferences. As with any mattress, the experience will depend on individual needs, bedding choices, and the type of foundation being used. Anyone planning to pair a mattress with an adjustable base should confirm compatibility with the manufacturer's guidance rather than assume that every foam mattress is suitable for repeated bending. Temperature Can Affect How the Bed Feels Over Time A mattress may feel comfortable when someone first lies down but noticeably warmer after several hours. Body heat, perspiration, bedding, and room conditions all influence this experience. Memory foam can maintain close contact with the body, and that contact may make warmth more noticeable for some sleepers. The result depends on the materials and construction involved, as well as how much heat and moisture build up in the sleeping environment. Couples can experience different temperature preferences even when sharing the same mattress. One person may feel comfortable beneath a heavier comforter, while the other wakes up warm and removes the covers. Separate blankets can make it easier to manage these differences without repeatedly pulling bedding across the bed. Breathable sleepwear, appropriately weighted bedding, and suitable room ventilation may also help. A memory foam mattress should be evaluated as part of this complete setup, since the mattress alone cannot control every source of nighttime warmth. Bedding Choices Matter When the Sides Move Independently Separate adjustment can create a practical problem when sheets and blankets are not suited to the bed's movement. A fitted sheet that is too tight may pull against the corners when one side rises, while loose bedding can bunch around the knees or waist. When one sleeper raises the head and the other remains flat, a shared blanket may also shift toward the lower side, leaving one person covered differently from the other. Using appropriately sized fitted sheets and bedding designed for the particular split king arrangement can reduce these issues. Some couples find that separate comforters work better than a single shared one because each person can adjust the covering without disturbing the other. It is also worth checking that bedding does not interfere with the moving sections of the foundation. Small changes to sheet fit and blanket placement can improve the experience without requiring a new mattress or a different adjustment routine. Creating a Routine That Works for Both Sleepers When bedtime schedules differ, a consistent routine can reduce unnecessary disturbance. The person going to bed later can prepare clothing, reading materials, and other items before entering the bedroom. Using a low-level light and avoiding repeated adjustments after the first sleeper has settled may also help. These measures cannot remove every disturbance, but they can make the transition between bedtime routines less disruptive. It can also help to agree on preferred positions before the night begins. One person might raise the head section for reading and return it to a comfortable sleeping position afterward, while the other settles into their usual setting. If the foundation has saved position settings, these may make it easier to return to familiar angles. Couples should still prioritise comfort over a fixed setting, because the position that works on one evening may not feel the same after a long day or a change in sleeping posture. Finding a Better Balance Between Individual and Shared Comfort Different bedtime routines do not have to mean that couples compromise on every aspect of sleep. Independent adjustment can help each person find a preferred position, while a suitable mattress can provide support as the body moves between positions. Still, the best results come from considering the complete arrangement: the foundation, mattress construction, bedding, bedroom conditions, and habits that influence how easily each person settles down. Memory foam's response to pressure changes throughout the night, but the amount of movement or warmth one sleeper notices depends on several factors. Couples can make the experience more predictable by checking compatibility, choosing bedding that works with independent movement, and agreeing on routines that minimize unnecessary disturbance. Instead of expecting one feature to resolve every issue, focus on how the setup performs during the actual bedtime patterns both people follow. That is a more reliable way to build a shared sleeping environment that accommodates individual preferences without overlooking common comfort needs.

articles.title: Jane Kim and Nithya Raman
articles.author: Randy Shaw
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. California and Los Angeles voters were on the same page last week. They wanted real change. Former San Francisco Supervisor Jane Kim was elected California Insurance Commissioner. Kim overcame millions of dollars in independent expenditures for Ben Allen, her opponent. She also overcame some of the nastiest newspaper attacks of this election cycle. In October I laid out the case for a Kim victory (See “ Can Jane Kim Win Race for Insurance Commissioner? “). I wrote, “I think California voters are fed up with the insurance industry. And they want to elect someone they see as committed to radically changing it. They see Jane Kim as that candidate. Not Ben Allen.” Longtime East Bay journalist Robert Gammon noted how this played out: “Crazy dynamics in the CA Insurance Commissioner race between two Dems. Lefty progressive Jane Kim is beating traditional liberal Ben Allen in nearly all of the ruby red Central Valley. The more moderate Allen is doing well along the liberal coast.” Related: Prop 40 and the Price of Progressive Disunity Liberal voters were likely swayed by Allen’s California Democratic Party endorsement. But that might have hurt him with Republicans. Kim had labor’s strong backing. She was also clearly the woman the insurance industry feared most. Voter anger at the insurance industry crossed political lines. And most voters wanted a fighter. My earlier story cited some of the attacks on Kim’s proposals. Some believe Kim will drive insurance companies out of the state. But one thing I learned about Jane Kim from her representing the Tenderloin as supervisor: she is very pragmatic. Like Bernie Sanders who has mentored her, Kim is less about ideology and more about getting things done. Raman Will Set New Course for LA Many will look at that heading and say, “Isn’t that what we thought would happen with Karen Bass? And Eric Garcetti? And Antonio Villaraigosa? Why should we expect anything different from Nithya Raman?” The big difference is how Raman got elected. Every council member who endorsed backed Bass. So did congress members, U.S. senators and state legislators. City Controller Kenneth Mejia, who ran as an outsider in 2022 and was re-elected in June, was the only city official to back Raman. He was joined by County Supervisor Lindsey Horvath. The other four county supervisors backed Bass. Incumbent Mayor Karen Bass was a longtime progressive. But she failed to bring real change. Related: Can Nithya Raman Surprise Karen Bass in LA Mayor’s Race? Unlike prior LA mayors Raman won’t feel hemmed him by powerful political backers. She barely had any. Raman can finally push Los Angeles to build the massive number of new housing units it desperately needs. She has a proven track record on housing and tenants rights and campaigned on that record. As I describe in Generation Priced Out , Los Angeles has the most politically powerful homeowners of any major city. They have prevented Los Angeles mayors from building apartments in or even near single-family home neighborhoods across the city. Mayor Bass conceded to their demands because she thought it would help get her re-elected. She was wrong. I suspect the progressive council members who backed Bass did so because they felt she would win. I can’t see them opposing Mayor Raman on key issues. From the day she announced her candidacy I felt Raman could win (See “ Can Nithya Raman Upset Karen Bass in LA Mayor’s Race? ,” February 17, 2026). On October 8 I laid out why Raman should prevail (See.” Nithya Raman Builds Momentum in LA Mayor’s Race “). But as election day neared, polls showed voters shifting to Bass. Impacted by my own experience rooting for outsider Tom Bradley in his failed 1969 runoff, I felt on the eve of Election Day that Los Angeles voters would again favor the status quo. I’ve never been happier to get a prediction wrong.

articles.title: Statement from UAW President Shawn Fain and UAW Vice President Ryan Hiestand on Delphi Retirees
articles.author: Justin Mayhugh
articles.content: The UAW is happy to announce that GM has agreed to honor its commitments to Delphi retirees who were denied annual lumpsum payments in 2023, 2024, 2025, and 2026. The remaining eligible Delphi retirees will receive a $2,000 payment in or about March 2027 covering prior years, and a future $500 payment in December 2027. Let’s be clear. This issue never should’ve taken this long to resolve. While GM makes a record $20 billion payout to Wall Street, certain Delphi retirees have had to wait years to get what they’ve been owed. Through the diligence of the UAW, and the members who raised their voices, we have made things right, and will keep fighting for every single member to get their fair share.

articles.title: Privatizing the VA
articles.author: Steve Early, Suzanne Gordon
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. If any Trump appointees lose their posts, as part of a mid-term cabinet re-shuffling, Secretary of Veterans Affairs (VA) Doug Collins is not likely to be among them. Unlike controversial former colleagues, already sacked as the heads of Homeland Security, Justice, and Labor Departments—or Pete Hegseth, the next to go?– Collins keeps his own head down. He does the president’s bidding, without personal drama or political scandal. This low-profile Air Force Reserve chaplain is a clean-living Southern Baptist minister, small town lawyer and former Congressman from Georgia. When the Senate confirmed him last year, there was no need for a tie-breaking vote like the one JD Vance cast to push Pete across the finish line as Secretary of Defense. The far more affable Collins won Senate approval with the bi-partisan support of twenty-two Democrats! They included Richard Blumenthal (D-CT), a military veteran whose own son is a VA patient and, sadly, were joined by Bernie Sanders (I-Vt), former chair of the Senate Veterans Affairs Committee (SVAC). Related: Veterans, Labor, and the Fight to Save the VA From Privatization Busting VA Unions Collins has proved to be Trump’s worst VA Secretary ever; his main goal is faster privatization of the nation’s largest public healthcare system. The likelihood that he will control the third largest federal agency budget and second largest departmental workforce, for another two years, is not good news for nine million VA patients. By the time any Democrat replaces Trump in January, 2029, Collins will have diverted far more than $46 billion annually, from their direct care budget to a network of 1.7 million private sector providers and four healthcare companies who administer it. Just two months ago, he awarded new contracts to the latter worth $1 trillion, over the next decade (if not cancelled or curtailed by a future administration). As a result, industry giants like United Healthcare and Humana will be profiting from further out-sourcing of VA care that is costly, unnecessary, and not favored by veterans themselves. VA defenders, inside and outside the Beltway, need a damage control agenda, that will restrain–rather than enable—further White House attempts to defund and dismantle our best working model of socialized medicine. Otherwise, more VA staffing and budget cuts, plus facility closings, in the VA’s own system of 1,380 public hospitals and clinics around the country will be happening soon. Reinforcements on the Way Those most motivated to lead the charge against Secretary Collins on Capitol Hill in 2027 are newly-elected pro-labor progressives, with personal experience in public health care systems, either as patients, their family members, care-givers, or administrators Thanks to their successful campaigns against MAGA supporters, these VA defenders now include: former Army paratrooper Ric hard Ojeda in North Carolina; former Marine drill instructor JoAnna Mendoza in Arizona who has been treated for military sexual trauma at the VA; former Army surgeon Adam Hamaway , a Gaza war critic from New Jersey, who once operated on a helicopter pilot injured in Iraq named Tammy Duckworth, now Senator from Illinois; and Fred Wellman from Missouri, a West Point graduate who began rallying fellow vets against Trump six years ago through the Lincoln Project. Last but not least is VA privatization critic Mitch Berman , “who spent over a decade serving veterans, active duty service members and their families as a VA nurse”—and now represents conservative Republican Paul Ryan’s old district in Wisconsin. Any of the above could help energize a House Veterans Affairs Committee, where playing footsie with Collins (and his Biden Administration predecessor) has gone on for too long, to the detriment of real agency oversight. On the SVAC, the Democrats’ defense of our nation’s largest public healthcare system would be much improved by adding new Senators from either Michigan, Maine, and Iowa. Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, the just elected Michigan public health specialist and Medicare for All advocate would be following in the footsteps of his big financial backer, Senator Bernie Sanders. Or El-Sayed could be joined by Troy Jackson, the former logger who ousted 5-term Senator Susan Collins with Sanders’ support; as a state legislator, Jackson long championed the cause of Maine National Guard members who suffered Agent Orange exposure during their Vietnam era training but were later deemed ineligible for compensation and healthcare. In Iowa, its newly elected Senator Josh Turek is not only the son of Vietnam veteran but one who suffered birth defects due to his father’s Agent Orange exposure. As a wheel-chair athlete, Turek played alongside disabled vets and worked with them in sports rehabilitation programs. He has pledged to “end unnecessary wars that put American lives at risk” and insure that “veterans exposed to toxic substances during their military service get the care and benefits they need.” Related: Who Controls the Union? CWA Members Fight a Trusteeship in Buffalo Ready, Fire, Aim A recent report from Democracy Forward –by two former VA officials–provides plenty of ammo for new members of Congress to use in a long-overdue counter-offensive against Collins. As Josh Jacobs, a former VA Under Secretary, under Joe Biden, and Nicole Nedd, a past director of the agency’s national workforce management program, report: In their indictment of Collins, entitled Ready, Fire, Aim , the authors warn that “the choices being made now by the Trump-Vance administration—at the White House and within VA’s own leadership—will adversely shape veterans’ care for a generation.” Road Map for Fighting Back Nobody new or old inside the Beltway—whether in Congress or veterans’ advocacy organizations–will get much done by themselves, without the pressure of grassroots opposition to cuts in VA care and benefits. Paul Reickhoff, an Iraq war veteran who helped found Iraq and Afghanistan Veterans of America (IAVA) two decades ago, believes that “both parties are looking for quiet ways to control VA disability spending, which now tops $118 billion a year for 5.1 million disabled veterans.” This fall, Reickhoff’s new group, Independent Veterans of America (IVA), backed candidates like Navy Veteran and former National Guard member Dan Osborn, who distanced themselves from both major parties. Unfortunately, Osborn suffered a second narrow defeat running as a labor-backed independent candidate for the U.S. Senate from Nebraska. Reickhoff fears that “career political operatives” in Washington are still floating “budget options” which include “cutting benefits and raising minimum disability rating thresholds.” To stop these changes, veterans have to “build the media and organizing muscle to mobilize fast when veterans’ benefits are on the line.” Fortunately, veterans’ groups, across the political spectrum, had a major victory earlier this year when they blocked the misleadingly-named “Take Care of America’s Veterans Act” (TACVA) . Veterans Service Organizations (VSOs) like the Veterans of Foreign Wars, Disabled American Veterans, and Progressive Veterans of America all sounded the alarm about this Collins-backed bill pushed by Republican House Speaker Mike Johnson. TACVA would have helped 50,000 former service members–whose careers were cut short due to medical problems–collect both their military pensions and VA disability benefits. But, as Common Defense Political Director Naveed Shah warned last summer, this multi-part bill was heavily booby trapped. If enacted, hundreds of thousands of other veterans would have been adversely affected. According to Shah, an Army veteran who served in Iraq, it would have “cut $57 billion from our future tinnitus and sleep apnea claims, tripled the VA home loan fee, allow disability appeals to be decided in bulk rather than on the merits of each veteran’s record, enable more lay-offs that threaten the quality of VA care, and lay the groundwork for handing VA facilities over to private operators.” (Lame-duck Republicans may make a second attempt to pass TACVA, in similarly problematic form, before January.) Related: ICE Killing in Maine Shows Why Vets Need Vetting—And Not Just in Politics Grassroots Defense of VA Care Veterans for Peace (VFP) has long been the most reliable first responder whenever veterans’ care has been threatened. VFP’s “Save Our VA” campaign has generated thousands of letters to members of Congress about privatization-related problems, too often downplayed or ignored by VSOs which take healthcare industry donations. VFP members have personally lobbied many members of Congress or their staffers on VA issues. A newer Common Defense campaign—called “VA Not For Sale”—has sponsored VA-focused lobby days in D.C. and town hall meetings in Iowa, Wisconsin, Illinois, and other states. CD and the Veterans Healthcare Policy Institute (VHPI) also collaborated on a just-issued report called The Privatization Playbook , which documents the whole sorry history of bi-partisan support for costly and unnecessary VA out-sourcing since 2014. In California, members of the Vietnam Veterans of America (VVA) and VFP have joined forces with active and retired VA care-givers to conduct weekly anti-privatization picketing and rallies at their local facility in Sonoma County. In 2027, there should be hundreds of events like this, in far more locations around the country. And, before it’s too late, more protests should target the costly and defective overhaul of VA medical record keeping, that’s occurring on Collins’ watch. Stopping Oracle’s Roll Out! As Ace Allen, a now retired VA medical oncologist, warned last spring in the Kansas City Star , in every place where the VA’s existing system has been “modernized” by Oracle-Cerner, the result has been serious disruption of patient record handling and widespread demoralization among VA care-givers forced to use an inferior system. As a result, “huge numbers have quit or retired early.” During the president’s first term, Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner helped Oracle-Cerner get a no-bid contract to replace what Allen calls a “custom built, publicly owned electronic health record (EHR) system that was refined over decades by VA clinician-coder teams to support clinical care, not maximize revenue.” A contract originally estimated to cost $10 billion has now ballooned to $32 billion in the same “cost-over-run” fashion as infamous Pentagon projects like the F-35 Joint Strike Fighter. That’s why Steve Friday, an Air Force veteran, VFP member and former VA social worker in Michigan, is helping to rally foes of Oracle-Cerner around the country through StopTheRollout.org . According to Friday, this grassroots initiative “brings together clinicians, VA employees, veterans, advocates, union members, and others who understand what is happening and are willing to act.” They are scouring contracting records, publicizing inspector general and GAO reports on Oracle-Cerner system failures, and sharing whistle-blower information, from patients and providers, with members of Congress willing to hold Collins responsible for already occurring patient safety threats. As Friday explains his involvement—and the stakes for everyone– “the VA, for all its problems, still demonstrates that we can publicly fund and deliver healthcare rather than turning every patient into a source of profit. “Losing that,” he says, “would hurt veterans, workers, and the larger struggle for healthcare as a human right.” Thanks to last week’s mid-term election results, this care-giver perspective will soon be much better reflected on Capitol Hill. Beyond Chron

articles.title: Slow-Motion Nuclear War
articles.author: Tom Engelhardt
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. In February 1982, in the New Yorker , Jonathan Schell imagined and described what a Russian twenty-megaton nuclear bomb (1,600 times the yield of the bomb that destroyed the Japanese city of Hiroshima at the end of World War II) might do if it hit New York City (his hometown and mine), though its radioactive fallout would have reached significantly farther. That one bomb, he wrote, “would probably doom upward of twenty million people.” He then described just what that nightmare might be like in all too vivid detail. (”If the wind was blowing at 15 miles an hour, fallout of lethal intensity would descend in a plume about 150 miles long and as much as fifteen miles wide.”) Given the nuclear arsenals that nine nations on this embattled planet of ours now possess (with undoubtedly more to come ), god knows what a nuclear war might be like so many years later, other than a potentially world-ending experience. Of course, since he wrote that, it’s become all too clear that we humans have managed to come up with a second way to do in this world of ours, which we’ve all too mildly labeled “climate change.” (Unfortunately, it won’t just be “change,” but a long-term catastrophe of an almost unimaginable kind.) Related: Donald Trump: The President of American Decline In many ways, climate change might be considered the equivalent of nuclear weapons already going off around this planet of ours, just in remarkably slow motion. And by the way, to give Schell full credit, more than 40 years ago, he was already aware of that phenomenon, too, writing then: “Nuclear explosions are far from being the only perturbations in question; a heating of the global atmosphere through an increased greenhouse effect, which could be caused by the injection of vast amounts of carbon dioxide into the air (for instance, from the increased burning of coal), is another notable peril of this kind. But a nuclear holocaust would be unique in its suddenness.” And at that time, he was almost uniquely focused on the two ways we humans could do ourselves in and on what he then so strikingly called “the fate of the Earth,” which sadly couldn’t have been more accurate or potentially worse. And yet so many years later, on a planet growing ever hotter ever faster and, in weather terms, ever more violent, we and our leaders still largely haven’t absorbed what’s happening, not truly. And because that potentially world-ending time frame is indeed proceeding in what might be considered slow motion (at least in comparison to the nuclear hell of atomic weaponry, although it’s happening far too fast for our world), it’s hard even to take in. Still, it’s important for us to start imagining that, in some strange sense, the equivalent of a slow-motion atomic war has already broken out on this planet of ours and the fallout (so to speak) is heat, heat, and more heat (and, of course, increasing weather chaos). Buy the Book Unfortunately, even so many years after Schell wrote that passage, because climate change is relatively slow, it simply hasn’t gotten the end-of-world attention it deserves. And yet, so many years later, the devastation is indeed beginning to be felt. Only recently, for instance, as a British Guardian —a rare news outlet that actually has a “ climate crisis” section — headline put it , “Heat killed ‘staggering’ 50,000 people in Europe’s cities this summer, scientists warn.” (”Hot weather marked by relentless heatwaves killed nearly twice as many people as it did in each of the two next most dangerous years.”) Yes, 50,000 deaths and, remember, that’s just in Europe (and it’s only going to get ever worse)! And the major power that’s still pouring fossil fuels into the atmosphere in a stunning fashion without, in the age of Donald J. Trump, making the slightest effort to promote green energy, is, of course, my country, the (increasingly dis-)United States of America. (At least, that other great power China, while itself still pouring stunning amounts of greenhouse gases into the atmosphere, is also hard at work creating and controlling the global green-energy market.) And imagine that, at just such a moment, my countrymen (and women) reelected as president a guy who openly insists that climate change is a made-up and fraudulent phenomenon, or as he put it at the United Nations last year, “the greatest con job ever perpetrated on the world.” The Fate of the Earth Today Someday, who will even believe how difficult it was for our version of humanity to take in the obvious disaster that was looming, even if (unlike the explosion of nuclear weapons) in slow motion? When, I wonder, will we indeed begin to think of climate change as a slow-motion version of atomic warfare? Try as a start just to take in those 50,000 dead people in Europe’s cities and then consider the fact (and it is a fact!) that that’s just the beginning. As long as we humans continue to fight wars (which pour fossil fuels into the atmosphere in a stunning fashion) and burn vast quantities of oil, natural gas, and coal to power our everyday lives (not to speak of the huge Artificial Intelligence data centers now being set up globally), things are only going to get so much worse. And mind you, while those 50,000 deaths were certainly reported in places like the New York Times , they weren’t generally considered headline or front-page news (or the TV or online equivalent thereof). And count on this: no one in the mainstream would ever use a headline like: “50,000 dead in equivalent of a slow-motion nuclear catastrophe.” Related: Why Does the World's Most Powerful Military Keep Losing Wars? But imagine this as well: those 50,000 dead are just the bare beginning of this nightmare, since we all know (or at least should know) that this planet, however slowly, is only going to get ever hotter, as our weather grows ever wilder and more brutal. That, of course, will be especially true if the major countries on this planet continue to be led by figures like Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin who simply don’t give a—and it’s an appropriately hellish word—damn about climate change. After all, “my” president has gone out of his way to dismiss the phenomenon, while essentially doing anything he could to further the use of oil, coal, and natural gas. Not surprisingly, he’s also slashing the budget and staff of, and taking a wrecking ball to, the agency in the government that has focused on the climate, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA). In that sense, though he’s seldom portrayed this way, he’s quite literally the president from hell. And (no surprise) climate change proved to generally be a hushed-up subject in the congressional races this time around. Likely as not, it won’t even be a significant issue in the next American presidential election either (especially, of course, if Donald Trump does run an unprecedented fourth time for an unprecedented and unconstitutional third term in office). In truth, we now need the TV, movie, and online equivalents of George Orwell’s 1984 or Aldous Huxley’s Brave New World for the climate. It’s as if—because it’s all happening in what passes for slow motion—we can’t fully (or in all too many cases, even partially) take in what’s happening to us and, worse yet, if you’re of a certain age (like me), what’s likely to happen in the undoubtedly far more violently overheating world that our children and grandchildren are likely to experience. Face it (if only we could!), strange as it may seem, the equivalent of a global atomic war has indeed broken out on this planet, just in slow motion, and it’s time to pay significant attention to it before everything gets so much worse. If only, back in 1982, readers had been paying more attention to Jonathan Schell when he began to focus on “the fate of the Earth,” we might indeed be in a far different situation today. articles.title: Providence Built a Winning Movement to Divest From Israel
articles.author: Zack Kligler
articles.content: The midterm elections saw progressive, pro-Palestine candidates sweep into office across the country on the back of public outrage at Israel’s ongoing genocide in Gaza. These victories should help reshape the conversation around Israel in Washington, reflecting the shifts in American public opinion against Israel that have acutely developed over the past three years. But that shift can be seen in other ways beyond electoral victories — like the passage of a binding ordinance last Tuesday in Providence, Rhode Island, divesting from Israel and other entities complicit in “ethnic cleansing, apartheid, illegal military occupation, or genocide.” The measure, which was listed on the ballot as Question 7, makes Providence the largest US city to divest from Israel and the first to enact a divestment law through popular vote. The first two years of Israel’s genocide in Gaza saw unsuccessful divestment campaigns both inside Providence City Hall and at Brown University. In 2024, Jewish Voice for Peace–Rhode Island (JVP-RI) launched a campaign to pass Israel bonds divestment legislation through city council. While the campaign had a long list of endorsers, a base of popular support, and the backing of three city councilors, Providence Mayor Brett Smiley (a darling of the Israel lobby) threatened to veto the measure and leaned on councilors to oppose it, ultimately succeeding in stymieing the effort. That same year saw massive student uprisings for divestment across the country, including a hunger strike and the Gaza Solidarity Encampment at Brown University. The university threatened disciplinary action against student protesters and charged them with criminal trespassing. In late 2025, as the “ceasefire” took effect in Gaza and energy for street protests and civil disobedience waned, the local anti-genocide movement in Providence was in a position to reassess our strategy. We had tried lobbying our leaders, and we knew our power lay in the overwhelming popular opposition to the US-backed genocide in Gaza. At the same time, broader political opportunities in Providence had opened up. In addition to standing in the way of divestment, Mayor Smiley also killed a rent stabilization bill after a hard-fought battle led by housing justice group Reclaim Rhode Island (Reclaim RI). Rhode Island has one of the worst homelessness crises in the country, and Providence consistently ranks among the least affordable cities for renters. In September, democratic socialist State Rep. David Morales announced a run for mayor, centering his campaign around housing and affordability. Morales was also joined by a growing slate of progressive city council candidates backed by Reclaim RI, including core JVP-RI organizer Jackie Goldman. Watching as this citywide socialist wave took shape, we knew we needed a vehicle to keep Palestine and the demand for divestment alive in this potentially transformative electoral cycle. Soon enough, organizers in nearby Somerville, Massachusetts, gave us our vehicle. In November 2025, Somerville for Palestine passed a nonbinding citywide Boycott, Divestment, and Sanctions (BDS) referendum, winning with 56 percent of the vote. This new and almost entirely untested tactic seemed to offer the answer to our problem. By bringing a similar citywide referendum, we could take the question of divestment directly to the people while building a positive feedback loop with candidates campaigning on affordability and immigration justice. A largely unused clause in Providence’s city charter allowed us to bring a binding ordinance to popular vote through a two-step petition process. After working with national movement leaders and legal experts and seeking advice from Somerville for Palestine as well as organizers in Pittsburgh who had attempted a similar referendum but failed to overcome legal challenges to their initial petition, we finalized an ordinance to be printed on thousands of petition sheets that would circulate into the spring and summer. During this process, JVP-RI pulled together a coalition of organizations to back the campaign under the banner of Providence for Palestine: Rhode Island Democratic Socialists of America, Reclaim RI, American Muslims for Palestine MA/RI, and American Federation of Teachers (AFT) Local 6516, which houses Brown University graduate workers, many of whom were involved in the previous divestment struggle at the university. A Ubiquitous Presence in Providence The campaign launched in February with about forty volunteers who slogged their way through two blizzards to collect the first thousand signatures required by the city charter to bring the ordinance to city council. In April, the council declined to pass the ordinance into law. Prepared for the council’s unwillingness to act and determined to bypass its authority by bringing the ordinance to popular vote, a rapidly growing base of volunteer petitioners set out to collect signatures from an additional 5 percent of the city’s registered voters. We soon became, according to one local reporter , “a ubiquitous presence at parks, farmers markets, and events” all summer long. The requirements of the petition were a blessing in disguise: they forced volunteers to get good at standing on street corners and talking to voters across the city about the relevance of the genocide in Gaza to local politics, the ethical virtues of divestment, and the power of local citizens to bypass elected officials on matters of grave moral importance. By the end of July, Providence for Palestine announced a tally of an additional 9,500 signatures gathered by almost 150 volunteers since the initial petition had been brought to city council in April. Morales and several of the other progressive candidates — including Goldman and Brittany Kubicek, who RI DSA was running as an independent socialist candidate for state representative — had already endorsed the petition effort before it got on the ballot, with some carrying petition sheets door to door as they canvassed their districts. By the time the city officially placed Question 7 on the ballot on July 30, divestment was already becoming a core plank of their collective platform. On September 9, the socialist wave crashed in Providence. Not only did Morales win the mayoral primary in a landslide — making Smiley the first incumbent mayor ever to lose a primary in Providence — but every single Reclaim-endorsed candidate won their primary, securing a progressive majority bloc on city council. In deep blue Rhode Island, almost all races are decided in the primary. That meant that between September 9 and November 3, divestment became the core electoral priority for the local left. Providence for Palestine absorbed many of the volunteers who turned out for socialist candidates and held over thirty canvasses between the primary and the general election. By November, we had reached out to almost thirty thousand voters to talk about divesting city funds. On election night, Question 7 won majorities in every one of the city’s fifteen wards, including in the most heavily Jewish neighborhoods. Where’s Next? Our victory in Providence was shaped by local conditions, but we believe it has potential to be a watershed moment for the BDS movement across the United States. The gap between the American public’s opposition to Israeli apartheid and our elected leaders’ continued support has never been wider. In both Somerville and Providence, ballot initiatives have proved a fruitful tactic to tap into popular outrage at the political establishment, build a mass base, and win concrete policy victories. This campaign also represented an evolution of the pro-Palestine movement’s relationship to the socialist electoral wave sweeping the country. Not only did the movement in Providence jump into the ring to support a candidate who aligned with our values, as we’ve seen occur in New York City and in Democratic primaries across the country; we forwarded our own policy priority and pulled socialist candidates into the campaign on the strength of its momentum. This is an expansion of the Palestine solidarity playbook and could make divestment an achievable demand in major US cities at the same time as pro-Palestine politicians work to end US military backing of Israel in Washington — a huge leap forward for the BDS movement. If Providence — a heavily Jewish city not previously viewed as a stronghold of left politics — can win divestment with 75 percent of the vote, we believe this is a winnable campaign in any city in the country. Where is next? This article originally appeared in Jacobin , a democratic socialist magazine publishing long-form essays and analysis on politics, economics, and culture. articles.title: Violence Against Women
articles.author: Lily Minh Wass
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. This September, independent student newspaper The Cornell Daily Sun broke news of a civil lawsuit brought forth by Jane Doe—a former student who dropped out following her alleged rape and assault by seven members of the Chi Phi fraternity in 2024. The story galvanized a nation of Jane Does, where one in four undergraduate women experience sexual assault after starting college. At Cornell University, that number recently rose to one in three. Survivors and allies took to social media, decrying how universities and legal systems have failed female student bodies for generations. But these same platforms were already rife with antifeminist groups, connected by a digital architecture that tends to favor outrage and intimidation. These male-exclusive spaces, whether in-person or online, share allegiance to a common myth: Masculinity, in the singular, weaponized definition, is under attack. This myth shaped American fraternities into the institutions we know today. The original fraternities of the early 1800s more closely resembled literary and debating societies, where students sought academic freedom outside their formal curriculum. As the turn of the twentieth century approached, affluent white men found themselves joined by women, the working-class, and racial minorities on campus, upending the exclusivity of educational institutions. Fraternities began shifting from their original intellectual focus to the preservation of male privilege, where hazing, the objectification of women, and secrecy formed the bond of brotherhood. The earliest recorded college hazing death took place at Cornell University in 1873, just three years after the university admitted its first female student. A century later, the myth of embattled masculinity resurged within the manosphere , an umbrella term for misogynistic communities online. “Red-pilled” users make reference to The Matrix to assert their belief in a “simulation” in which feminism systematically oppresses contemporary men. The rest of the world is said to remain “blue-pilled”—ignorant of the truth. In both centuries, qualms with the changing present have been used to create a nostalgia for an idealized past premised on patriarchy and bigotry. By building an insular, self-affirming ecosystem, grievance by grievance, these spaces also mobilize sufficient influence to impose their unreality on the rest of us. Related: Big Tech’s Next Dark Pattern: Turning AI Users Into the Product In a widely publicized image from Jane Doe’s lawsuit, the accused are seen inviting fifty-seven fraternity brothers in their Snapchat group chat to participate in the rape. The secrecy of this exchange was protected by Snapchat’s ephemerality, which erases unsaved texts after twenty-four hours, and the fraternity’s code of silence. None of the fifty- seven brothers who received these messages intervened on Jane Doe’s behalf. After defendant Jonathan Newell advertised “free p—sy” to the chat, defendant Scott Kretzschmar responded, “first person POV not a bit,” likely in reference to a style of online pornography. The defendants’ use of Snapchat is a prime example of what differentiates campus rape in the twenty-first century from its long-enduring precedent. Beyond the physical encounter of sexual assault, victims now face digital harms through the circulation of non-consensual intimate imagery (NCII), “dogpiling” and doxxing, and the use of generative artificial intelligence for prolonged harassment. When details of Jane Doe’s case went public two years after the alleged incident, right- wing influencers quickly sought to unmask her identity. A name that began circulating received so much attention that Instagram automatically labeled it a “popular” search term. Jane Doe has since dealt with nonstop threats, including swatting—a false call made to the police with the intention of leading SWAT teams to storm her family’s home. These mobilized extremists are continuing the online violence that first began in the Chi Phi Snapchat group on the night of Jane Doe’s assault. They’re aided by a web of anonymous networks to continuously harass victims like Doe. A prime example of these communities is the Burnerverse on X. On the surface, the Burnerverse is a site where X users convene to discuss university sports teams. Yet some of these “burner” accounts also take advantage of anonymity and Elon Musk’s lax content moderation policies to harass young women on college campuses. As a freshman at the University of Florida, Maddie Kowalski learned that X users had uploaded NCII and videos of her that quickly surpassed 8.5 million views. Kowalski told Wired that she had not consented to any of the acts in the footage circulating online, let alone to them being filmed and posted. Some of the X users amplifying this content were her classmates. Others were completely unaffiliated men. A year after the incident, searching her name on X, Google, and Instagram still brings up autocomplete suggestions for NCII of Kowalski. These are digital traces of the hidden, decentralized network that made her assault go viral, infecting enough corners of the internet to never disappear. The problem is not limited to X’s platform, college students, or even the United States. This same year has also brought horrifying revelations from CNN’s investigation into an “ online rape academy ”: Men around the world drugging and assaulting their unconscious partners, then uploading videos and tips to Telegram. What has remained consistent is the digital platforms’ willingness to lend their services to these crimes, amplifying and profiting from harmful content when it emerges. Related: How AI Sycophancy Fuels Technofascism and Undermines Critical Thinking Meta, X, and YouTube have all been found to run ads for explicit deepfake services, including depictions of child sexual abuse material (CSAM) . YouTube alone directed 1.82 million visits to “nudify” sites between December 2025 and March 2026. These same algorithms have brought misogynist forums from the fringes of the internet to the epicenter. Researchers at Dublin City University used blank smartphones to set up social media accounts, posing as teenagers, and then searched for “gender-normative” male content, like sports and video games. Within twenty-six minutes, their TikTok and YouTube accounts were flooded with toxic and manosphere posts . At the same time, women’s health organizations are sounding the alarm over the suppression of sexual and reproductive health information online . Creators report being removed and shadowbanned for posts containing terms like “vagina,” “pregnancy,” and “endometriosis.” When pressed for answers as to why women’s health gets censored while harassment, NCII, and CSAM filter through, social media companies have been quick to place responsibility on AI-driven content moderation. Meta has said it intends to replace 90 percent of its content review staff with automation by the end of this year. The company’s own chatbot has been found to obstruct access to information about abortion and other reproductive health issues, while alternatives like ChatGPT and Claude have returned misinformation and anti-abortion sources on the same topics. It’s an alarming red flag regarding who these algorithms work for and against. These same companies reap vast economic benefits from generative models trained on the public’s thoughts and images, even when data collection may infringe on copyrights and expectations of privacy . They now profit from the advertising of and engagement with misogyny. When platforms sidestep responsibility, they frame this exploitative structure as the only way forward. To benefit from the promise of the internet, we are told to give up our consent, privacy, and safety—some of us more than others. This framing is eerily reminiscent of what women have always heard: Your suffering is but a necessary price to pay. Girls and women shoulder this burden to attend university, to pursue a career, to use the internet. For Jane Does all over the world and the web, this cannot be the only way.
